title: Diwali Returns to London's National Maritime Museum With a New Bazaar
excerpt: The free 'All Together Now' festival on 7 November adds a Diwali Bazaar of South Asian designers to a programme of performances, workshops and talks in Greenwich.
body:
• The National Maritime Museum in Greenwich will host "All Together Now," a free Diwali festival on 7 November 2026, running from 10:00 to 17:00.
  • A new Diwali Bazaar — the first at the festival — will bring South Asian designers, makers and independent businesses into the museum's Ocean Court.
  • The programme includes Punjabi dhol, bhangra, Bharatanatyam, Rajasthani folk dance, rangoli workshops, sari-making displays and a lantern parade through Greenwich Park.
  • Curator Mehala Ford notes the museum has marked Diwali as a free public celebration for 16 years, spotlighting British South Asian creativity.

The National Maritime Museum in Greenwich will celebrate Diwali with a free, day-long festival on 7 November 2026 — and this year, for the first time, the celebration will include a dedicated Diwali Bazaar of South Asian designers, makers and independent businesses.

The festival, titled All Together Now and curated by Mehala Ford, founder of COMMONGROUND& and the Friday Sari Project, will run from 10:00 to 17:00 and showcase South Asian artists, performers, storytellers, makers and community organisations from across the UK. It is Ford's fourth year curating the event, and the museum says it has been celebrating Diwali as a free public event for 16 years.

A new addition: the Diwali Bazaar

The centrepiece addition for 2026 is the Diwali Bazaar, open from 11:00 to 16:00 in the museum's Ocean Court. Visitors can browse stalls featuring jewellery, clothing, prints, accessories, gifts and handmade products from South Asian creatives alongside local Greenwich-based businesses.

The bazaar is the festival's first dedicated shopping experience, and it lands as Diwali increasingly doubles as a moment for Britain's South Asian independent brands to reach a mainstream audience.

Performances across the Ocean Map

The museum's Ocean Map will host live music and dance throughout the day. Musician and sound therapist Kiran SKG opens the festival with a solo flute performance at the Stanhope Entrance at 09:50, followed by dance artist Nandita Shankardass and the Welcome Movement, Pooja Rajguru's Folk Mandali with traditional Rajasthani folk dance and Gujarati garba, and Bharatanatyam dancer Sweta Pandey.

Eternal Taal, an all-female group of dancers and dhol drummers, will bring the sounds of Punjab to the museum, while Bhangra4Us leads a bhangra performance and workshop. The day closes with a lantern parade through Greenwich Park at 17:15, accompanied by Eternal Taal's drummers; visitors can carry lanterns made in the day's workshops.

Workshops, talks and family activities

Hands-on programming includes a rangoli art workshop with Ekta Kaur of Story Beyond Lines, lotus lantern making, Button Masala's no-cut, no-stitch sustainable textile workshop, block printing, and a "Dress Up for Diwali" station where visitors can try on traditional South Asian clothing. The Saree Project stall and an "I Used to Be a Saree" display explore the cultural significance of the sari and its creative reuse.

The talks programme in the Lecture Theatre includes a panel on heritage, identity and belonging drawn from the museum's Home + Land podcast, a South Asian Salon conversation on Diwali food traditions, a Brown Game Strong panel on fashion and identity, and a Ramayana puppet theatre for children. Museum curator Aaron Jaffer will also present his new book, Black and Asian Seafarers: A Visual History, drawn from the museum's Unlocking Collections project.

Sixteen years of celebration

Ford said curating the festival remains a privilege, and that the day offers "a sensory experience of celebration" and a chance to discover the talents of South Asian communities.

"Curating Diwali at the Museum is always an honour and a privilege for me. Royal Museums Greenwich has been celebrating Diwali as a free public celebration for 16 years, which is incredible."

— Mehala Ford, founder of COMMONGROUND& and curator of the festival

For Britain's Indian and South Asian communities, the festival has become a fixture of the autumn calendar — a mainstream institution marking the Festival of Lights without a ticket price attached, alongside programming that reflects how the diaspora actually lives Diwali now: food conversations, identity panels and sustainable fashion sitting comfortably next to dhol drums and garba.

The full programme is listed at rmg.co.uk/diwali. Admission is free.
image_caption: Dancers in red and white traditional dress perform at the National Maritime Museum's Diwali celebration as a large crowd looks on. This year's festival, All Together Now, runs on 7 November and adds a first-ever Diwali Bazaar to the free day-long programme.
nri_angle: The festival is aimed squarely at Britain's Indian and South Asian communities, with programming — food talks, identity panels, sustainable fashion — that reflects how the diaspora keeps Diwali today.
author: Diaspora Desk
